podcast.body: Damon Albarn notably refused to license "Song 2" for use in a commercial for the US military, demonstrating a boundary for its commercial applications despite its widespread usage elsewhere. "The only place where the song didn't reach was a commercial for the US military. Damon Alburn refused to let them have it."

podcast.body: Despite its quick creation, "Song 2" became Blur's most enduring hit, generating millions in royalties. The ad-libbed "woohoo!" parts were especially valuable. It has been covered by numerous artists and extensively licensed for TV commercials (Toyota, BMW, Labatt, Intel), video games, movie trailers, TV shows, and almost every type of sporting event. "Turns out those ad-hawk woohoo's were worth millions and millions of dollars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: During recording, two drum kits, intentionally tuned to sound "cheap and trashy," were set up facing each other, played by Graham Coxon and Dave Rowntree. The band decided to play basic parts in the verses and "go to town" in the chorus. Damon Albarn, having only scraps of lyrics, ad-libbed the famous "woohoo!" parts, which were kept due to their unexpected effectiveness. "No one knew they were coming, but they sounded good so they kept them."

podcast.body: This track, always known as "Song 2," never received a proper title, coincidentally being the second song on the album, two minutes and two seconds long, and reaching number two on the British charts. It was conceived and recorded in under 30 minutes, performed and recorded in real time. "Yes, it's the second song on the record. And yes, it's two minutes and two seconds long. And yes, it reached number two in the British charts, but all those things are just coincidences."
